title: A quantum game of telephone
authors: Arefur Rahman, Matthew L. Stevens, Cory M. Nunn, Daniel E. Jones, Brian T. Kirby, Joseph M. Lukens
abstract: Characterizing multinode quantum networks without ubiquitous local entanglement sources presents significant experimental challenges. We introduce ``quantum telephone,'' an iterative ancilla-assisted process tomography protocol that leverages intermediate detection events, effectively treating previously probed links as ancillae for subsequent links. Implemented on a deployed multinode fiber network, we observe noisy intermediate channels create fundamental parameter degeneracies that compound inference errors under sequential estimation. Counterintuitively, the inclusion of downstream near-unitary channels provides boundary constraints that, when used in tandem with global inference, can resolve ambiguity in channels earlier in the sequence. By compensating for localized information loss, this approach obviates the strict full-rank requirements of standard ancilla-assisted process tomography, even when intermediate states become completely depolarized. Overall, quantum telephone offers a hardware-efficient and information-maximizing path toward characterizing complex quantum networks with limited resources.
summary: This paper introduces 'quantum telephone,' an advanced tomography protocol designed to characterize unknown quantum channels in multi-node networks using only intermediate detection events. By employing a global inference strategy rather than sequential estimation, the method overcomes fundamental limitations related to information loss and rank deficiency in noisy physical systems. This offers a robust pathway for building and verifying complex quantum communication infrastructure.
main_problem: The primary challenge is characterizing unknown quantum channels within complex, multi-node quantum networks when local entanglement sources are scarce.
main_result: A global inference protocol, termed 'quantum telephone,' successfully resolves parameter degeneracies and estimates channel parameters even when intermediate states become completely depolarized, outperforming sequential estimation methods.
method: The authors developed an iterative ancilla-assisted process tomography protocol that uses Bayesian inference (MCMC) to estimate the entire set of unknown channels simultaneously, leveraging global constraints from all measured links.
model_or_system: The work is implemented on a deployed multinode fiber network using polarization qubits across a three-node circular topology. The model involves characterizing sequential quantum processes $E_t$ connecting nodes (Alice, Bob, Charlie).
key_observables: Coincidence counts ($N_t$), process purities ($\hat{P}_t$), and estimated two-qubit density matrices ($\hat{ho}_{ij}$).
important_parameters: Depolarization probability ($p$), number of nodes (two vs. three), and the computational complexity difference between sequential and global inference.
main_assumptions: Standard ancilla-assisted process tomography requires full Schmidt rank, which is violated in general; the authors assume that global constraints can compensate for this local failure.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup (Fig 2), compare estimated channel purities vs. depolarization probability for sequential vs. global methods (Fig 3), and show process fidelities ($\hat{F}$) versus $p$ comparing fixed vs. variable unitary corrections (Figs 6 & 7).
paper_structure: The paper introduces the quantum telephone protocol, compares its performance against standard sequential estimation using both purity and fidelity metrics across two-node and three-node setups, and concludes by analyzing the implications of global versus local information gathering.
why_interesting: It provides a practical, hardware-efficient technique for characterizing complex open quantum systems (quantum channels) in real-world photonic networks, directly addressing resource limitations common in quantum networking research.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic of a three-node quantum telephone ex- periment. A central nonlinear source generates polarization- entangled photon pairs, which are distributed as bipar- tite states {ρ0A, ρBA, ρBC, ρA′ C} (colored lines) after opti- cal channels {E0, EA, EB, EC} (crimson arrows) to three nodes: Alice (A/A′), Bob (B), and Charlie (C). Bootstrapping on a single ancilla channel at Alice, all unknown quantum chan- nels are then inferred using the measured data, the accuracy of which depends on both the ground truth channels and the estimation procedure.

FIG. 2. Schematic of the experimental setup. Details are pro- vided in the text. EPC: electronic polarization controller; PA: polarization analyzer; PC: personal computer; PPSF: peri- odically poled silica fiber; SNSPD: superconducting nanowire single-photon detector; SPAD: single-photon avalanche diode; SW: switch; TT: time tagger; WRN: White Rabbit node; WRS: White Rabbit switch.

FIG. 3. Process purities ˆPA, ˆPB, ˆPC, and ˆPA′ as a function of depolarization probability p of the targeted ground truth Al- ice channel E⋆ A. (a) Two-node configuration. (b) Three-node configuration. Left and right columns delineate between se- quential inference via Eq. (3) and global inference via Eq. (4). Channels ˆEA and ˆEA′ should be compared to a depolarizing channel [Eq. (10)], while ˆEB and ˆEC should be compared to unitary channels [Eq. (9)].

FIG. 4. Real parts of the two-qubit density matrices ˆρij esti- mated directly from telephone coincidence counts, for p = 1 depolarizing probability on channel E⋆ A(A′). (a) Two-node tele- phone experiment. (b) Three-node telephone experiment.

FIG. 5. Resolving channel ambiguities through global quan- tum telephone. Observing a maximally mixed output state ρAB = (EA ⊗EB)(|ψ+⟩⟨ψ+|) leaves ambiguity as to the qual- ity of EA and EB. However, seeing a maximally entangled ρBC = (EB ⊗EC)(|ψ+⟩⟨ψ+|) requires that both EB and EC are unitary channels, information that can then be backprop- agated to reveal only EA as noisy.
